questions.scenario: A payments workload has separate production and development teams. A development administrator must never be able to change production resources, even after a mistaken broad IAM policy. What is the strongest first isolation boundary?

options.text: Separate AWS accounts under one organization.
Different tags in one account.
Different subnets in one VPC.
Different CloudWatch dashboards.

questions.explanation: AWS accounts are strong resource and permissions boundaries and limit the blast radius of accidental policies. Learn more in [Organizing your AWS environment](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/organizing-your-aws-environment/benefits-of-using-multiple-aws-accounts.html).

questions.scenario: An application and database are placed in one subnet named private-app. The requirement says the service must tolerate an Availability Zone failure. What is the decisive problem?

options.text: A subnet spans every Availability Zone in its Region.
A subnet belongs to one Availability Zone, so this placement is still single-AZ.
Private subnets cannot contain databases.
Availability Zones are global rather than regional.

questions.explanation: Each subnet is scoped to one Availability Zone. Tolerating an AZ failure requires placement across AZ-specific subnets. Learn more in [AWS fault isolation boundaries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-fault-isolation-boundaries/regions.html).

questions.scenario: A team creates an S3 bucket in eu-west-2, then runs an EC2 describe command against us-east-1 and sees no instances. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The account changed when the Region changed.
Availability Zones share names across every account.
Most service resources are regional, so the CLI Region scopes the request.
IAM policies are stored separately in each Region.

questions.explanation: Most resources are regional, and client configuration determines which regional endpoint receives a request. Learn more in [AWS Regions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-fault-isolation-boundaries/regions.html).

questions.scenario: Two accounts both show an Availability Zone named us-east-1a. Can the networking team assume those labels identify the same physical AZ?

options.text: Yes, letter names are globally fixed.
Yes, but only inside AWS Organizations.
No, because an AZ can move between Regions.
No. Use AZ IDs when coordinating physical-zone alignment across accounts.

questions.explanation: Account-specific AZ names can map differently. AZ IDs provide consistent cross-account identification. Learn more in [AWS fault isolation boundaries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-fault-isolation-boundaries/regions.html).

questions.scenario: A platform team adopts separate workload accounts. Which practices make the boundary usable without returning to long-lived IAM users?

options.text: Use IAM Identity Center for human access.
Share one root-user access key across accounts.
Use cross-account roles with narrow trust and permissions.
Use resource names as the only isolation control.
Centralize audit evidence with organization-aware logging.

questions.explanation: Identity Center, cross-account roles, and centralized evidence support multi-account operation. Root credentials should not become routine access. Learn more in [IAM best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html) and [multi-account guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/organizing-your-aws-environment/benefits-of-using-multiple-aws-accounts.html).
